newsitem.title: USA: Bill aims to cap public costs of Milwaukee stadium.
newsitem.headline: Bill aims to cap public costs of Milwaukee stadium.

text.p: A Wisconsin state senator is drafting a bill that would limit the amount of tax revenues used to help finance a $250 million ballpark for the Milwaukee Brewers baseball team.

Mike Boerger, an aide to Senate Republican Leader Michael Ellis, R-Neenah, said Thursday the bill would limit the financing share of the Southeast Wisconsin Professional Baseball Park District board, which is overseeing the project, to $160 million, plus financing costs.

Boerger said the bill would allow the state-created district to issue $160 million of debt backed by a 0.1 percent, five-county sales tax. However, sales tax revenues would be limited to paying off the bonds and not for paying off any future debt beyond the $160 million or to pay for cost overruns for the stadium.
In a Feb. 18 letter to Robert Trunzo, the district's chairman, Ellis said the Brewers "will be responsible for cost overruns and my legislation will make that a certainty."

Ellis cited a Feb. 11 credit report from Moody's Investors Service that said the district "will have to shoulder excess costs" of the project. In that report, Moody's gave an A3 rating to $146.7 million of long-term bonds the district plans to sell soon.
Yaffa Rattner, a Moody's analyst, said the bill would not impact the rating on the bonds "given the fact the security of the bondholders is not married to the fortunes of the stadium."
"Sales tax revenues will be collected as long as a dollar of debt is outstanding," she said.
If the bill were to become law, Rattner said the district and the Brewers would have to live within the $250 million budget for the project.

A reaction to the bill from the district was not immediately available. However, Patrick Born, a senior vice president at Evensen Dodge Inc., the district's financial adviser, said the bill could illegally conflict with an agreement between the district and the team that gives the district the responsibility for cost overruns.

Boerger pointed out the Brewers have yet to "put up a dime of their own money" for the stadium, whose cost was originally supposed to be split with the public paying $160 million and the team paying $90 million.

The team's inability to secure a bond-financed loan from a state bonding agency led to a new plan that provided $50 million in loans to the Brewers from the city of Milwaukee, the local business community and two foundations, and $40 million from the sale of naming rights, upfront concession payments and a letter of credit from the American Baseball League.
In his letter to the district's chairman, Ellis said that the legislation allowing the district to help finance the project limited the state's moral obligation pledge to $160 million of bonds.

However, the district in December sold $146.7 million of convertible option bonds without the state's pledge. The restructuring of those bonds into long-term debt, scheduled for early March, will carry MBIA Insurance Corp. insurance and no state pledge, according to Born.

Boerger said the bill's intent would be to keep the public participation in the project to no more than the $160 million level called for in the original legislation. He added that he was not sure when the bill would be completed or if it would attract co-sponsors.
A comment on the bill from Standard & Poor's Corp., which rated the upcoming bond issue A-minus, was not immediately available.
